area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how wind, bank and groundspeed shape the ground track in the rectangular course, S-turns and turns around a point, demonstrate any of them from the right seat while explaining it (altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, entry 600 to 1,000 feet AGL), and spot, explain and fix the errors your learners make.
why: Ground reference maneuvers are where a learner first flies a path over the ground instead of just an attitude, and the same skills run from every takeoff to every landing [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. They are flown low, with traffic, towers and a possible engine failure close at hand [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. As the instructor you set up the wind picture, fly it while talking, and catch the drift, coordination or altitude error before it becomes a habit or a low-level stall.

warmup: Think first: your learner flies turns around a silo holding a perfect 30° bank and a centered ball the whole way around, yet the circle over the ground comes out egg-shaped and slides off to one side. The learner insists the turn was flown correctly. What exactly did the learner do right, what did the learner miss, and how would you show it in the air so the learner sees it rather than just hears it?

key_terms.def: The path the airplane actually traces over the ground. In wind it differs from the path through the air [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Sideways movement over the ground caused by the moving air mass. A direct crosswind drifts the airplane at the full wind speed; a wind 45° off the nose, at just over 70 percent of it [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
The angle the nose is pointed into the wind to cancel drift. It depends on the wind speed, the wind's angle to the airplane and the airspeed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Speed over the ground. Lower than airspeed headed upwind, higher headed downwind [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
A turn that keeps the same distance from a ground reference. In wind it needs a bank that changes with groundspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Degrees of heading change per second: 1,091 x tangent of bank / airspeed in knots [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
Speed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank), in feet with speed in knots. Double the speed and the radius goes up four times [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
A maneuver that keeps an equal distance from all sides of a rectangular reference, flown to replicate the airport traffic pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
Two opposite but equal half-circles on each side of a straight-line reference, with wings level as the line is crossed [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].
Consecutive 360° constant-radius turns around one ground reference point [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Absorption in one task to the exclusion of others; often a sign that the task has not been practiced enough on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
The load on the wings in G units. A level 45° turn gives 1.41 G and a 60° turn 2.0 G; stall speed rises with the square root of it [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedures and the CFI standard

body.p: Purpose: ground reference maneuvers teach a pilot to hold the airplane on a chosen path over the ground, not just at an attitude. They combine the four fundamentals into the skills used from every takeoff to every landing, and they are the basis for traffic patterns and for jobs such as survey, photography and crop dusting [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. Introduce them as soon as the pilot shows proficiency in the four fundamentals [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

bullets: Procedures common to all three maneuvers: clear the area with two 90° clearing turns, complete the checklist, make any radio calls such as on a practice area frequency, and pick an emergency landing spot [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Fly them generally between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and always enter from a downwind position so the steepest bank comes first [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
Keep the bank at 45° or less and the airspeed at or below maneuvering speed; before the flight, look up the POH/AFM stall speed at 50° or the highest bank expected [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Use brief scans of the flight instruments; the main references are the natural horizon and the ground [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

head: What the evaluator sees
CFI ACS wording
rows: Select a suitable ground reference area, line, or point as appropriate. (ACS AI.IX.E.S2)
Plan the maneuver: rectangular course, S-turns or turns around a point, each entered 600 to 1,000 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a to S3c, taught in chunk 4)

Apply adequate wind-drift correction during straight and turning flight to maintain a constant ground track around a rectangular reference area, or to maintain a constant radius turn on each side of a selected reference line or point. (ACS AI.IX.E.S4)

If performing S-Turns, reverse the turn directly over the selected reference line; if performing turns around a point, complete turns in either direction, as specified by the evaluator. (ACS AI.IX.E.S5)
Divide attention between airplane control, traffic avoidance and the ground track while maintaining coordinated flight. (ACS AI.IX.E.S6)
Maintain altitude ±100 feet; maintain airspeed ±10 knots. (ACS AI.IX.E.S7)
Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task. (ACS AI.IX.E.S8)

body.p: What is new for you: the private ACS uses the same words for S1 to S7 (ACS PA.V.B.S1 to S7), so your private learners are held to exactly the numbers you demonstrate. The CFI Task adds 'procedures' to K1, adds K5 (common errors) and S8, and asks you to demonstrate and simultaneously explain. The evaluator selects at least one of the three maneuvers for you to demonstrate (ACS AI.IX.E note).

callout.text: For an ASEL CFI test the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, and Task E (this one) and Task F (Eights on Pylons) are always among them (ACS Area IX note). Expect to be asked for this Task.

check.q: Your private learner asks whether the CFI flies ground reference maneuvers to tighter numbers. What do you tell them?
check.a: No. The CFI and private ACS use the same S1 to S7 words, including altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.IX.E.S7, PA.V.B.S7). What the CFI adds is explaining while flying and analyzing and correcting errors (ACS AI.IX.E.S8).

body.p: Effects of wind on ground track: the airplane moves with the air mass. At 90 knots with a 10-knot wind from the right, it drifts 10 nautical miles left every hour, and at 180 knots it still drifts 10 [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. To hold a straight track, angle the nose into the wind just enough to cancel the drift. The needed angle depends on the wind speed, the wind's angle to the airplane, and the airspeed: at 100 knots, a 20-knot direct crosswind takes about 12°, a 10-knot one about 6° [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

bullets: Relation to a ground reference: a direct crosswind drifts the airplane at the wind's full speed; a wind 45° off the nose drifts it at just over 70 percent of the wind speed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Groundspeed: headed upwind it is lower than airspeed, headed downwind it is higher. The closer the wind is to the nose or tail, the bigger the effect on groundspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Pilots do not calculate drift corrections for these maneuvers; they use the references and adjust until the drift stops [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Teach eyes outside, not math.
Finding the wind: windsocks, smoke from factories or houses, dust, brush fires, wind farms, or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

body.p: The first lesson starts on a straight line. Track directly over a long road or railroad, or over at least three references that line up, angling into the wind to cancel drift, and scan from far ahead to close in. Then fly a parallel path offset from the line, no more than three-fourths of a mile away [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Only then move to the turning maneuvers.

callout.text: Known to unknown (application): the AFH compares the airplane to a boat crossing a river, where a slower boat or faster current needs a bigger angle upstream [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Learners who drive can relate it to a car on a windy bridge. Use what they already know, then show it over the road.

check.q: Your learner tracks a road with a 20-knot wind 45° off the nose and expects to drift at about 10 knots. What do you correct?
check.a: A wind 45° off the nose drifts the airplane at just over 70 percent of the wind speed, about 14 knots, not half [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. But the learner should not be computing it at all: watch the references and adjust until the drift stops [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

chunks.title: Bank, groundspeed, rate and radius of turn

body.p: Effects of bank angle and groundspeed on rate and radius of turn start with the formulas. Rate of turn = 1,091 x tangent of bank / airspeed in knots, and radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. More bank gives a faster rate and a smaller radius; more speed gives a slower rate and a larger radius, and doubling the speed makes the radius four times bigger [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

In no wind a fixed bank draws a circle over the ground. In wind the radius over the ground grows as groundspeed rises and shrinks as it falls, so a constant radius needs a bank that changes with groundspeed: steepest where groundspeed is highest, headed downwind, and shallowest headed upwind [[24:149|AFH 7-3]] [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. At higher groundspeed there is less time to turn, so the steeper bank raises the rate of turn to make up for it [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

head: Worked example (application of [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]])
Downwind
Upwind
rows: Hold 30° of bank all the way around
Wide, swinging away from the point

body.p: That is why the warmup learner's perfect 30° turn came out egg-shaped. The AFH gives its own worked numbers (an 890-foot circle needing about 45° downwind and 33° upwind) [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]; the Steep Spiral lesson (AI.IX.B) works those through, so use fresh numbers for your own airplane here.

callout.text: Size the circle for the wind. If the downwind bank comes out too steep, exit at once and set up farther from the reference; avoid banks over 45° because the stall speed rises [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
Fast over the ground, steep. Slow over the ground, shallow. The bank follows the groundspeed, not the heading.

check.q: Your learner says the bank must be steeper downwind 'because the airplane is going faster through the air.' What do you correct?
check.a: The airspeed is the same all the way around; it is the groundspeed that is higher downwind [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. The radius over the ground grows with groundspeed, so the bank must steepen to hold it [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

chunks.title: Picking the area, the reference and the entry

body.p: Select a suitable ground reference area, line, or point by thinking about the maneuver, the altitude, emergency landing options, the density of structures, the wind direction, the visibility and the type of airspace [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. Examples include roads, railroad tracks, fence lines, field boundaries, canals and water tanks [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

bullets: Altitude: generally 600 to 1,000 feet AGL. Lower altitudes make the airplane seem faster over the ground, and drift must be easy to see from both sides [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Obstructions: at least 500 feet vertically and 2,000 feet horizontally [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

People and animals: well away from open air assemblies, congested areas of a city, town or settlement, and herds of livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Over a congested area 14 CFR requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet; elsewhere 500 feet above the surface, or 500 feet from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure over sparse areas; and anywhere, an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

Illusions: large objects look closer than small ones, clear air makes references look closer than haze does, rain can make you feel higher than you are, and bright objects look closer than dim ones. References of similar size and proportion make the maneuvers easier [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

body.p: Plan the maneuver: the ACS sets the entry for each one (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a to S3c). The AFH adds how to make that entry work.

head: Sub-item
ACS entry
Planning from the AFH
rows: Enter a left or right pattern, 600 to 1,000 feet AGL at an appropriate distance from the selected reference area, 45° to the downwind leg
A square or rectangular field with references on all four sides; fly outside the boundaries, one-half to three-fourths of a mile away, so the edges are visible from either seat [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Enter perpendicular to the selected reference line, 600 to 1,000 feet AGL at an appropriate distance from the selected reference area
A straight line long enough for the turns, crossed at 90° from the downwind position [[24:155|AFH 7-9]]

A prominent point, easy to see but small enough to be precise; enter downwind at the planned radius [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]

callout.text: Before each ground reference maneuver, ask the learner to name the collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. It makes S2 a risk decision, not just a scenery choice.

check.q: Your learner picks a water tower at the edge of a small town for turns around a point at 700 feet AGL. What is wrong?
check.a: The AFH wants the area well away from congested areas [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and over a congested area 14 CFR 91.119(b) requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. Pick a reference out over open country instead.

chunks.title: Rectangular course: fly it, then teach it

body.p: Rectangular course: the airplane keeps an equal distance from all sides of the reference at a constant altitude and airspeed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Enter on the downwind leg at the ACS 45° to it (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a). Each corner is different because the wind changes from tailwind to crosswind to headwind [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. AI.IV.A (Maneuver Lesson) has the corner-by-corner table; here is how to read it from the right seat.

bullets: Two corners are more than 90° of turn (downwind to base, crosswind to downwind) and two are less (base to upwind, upwind to crosswind), because of the crab carried on the crosswind legs [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].
Roll rate is a wind tool: when the wind would drift the airplane into the course, roll in slowly; when it would drift the airplane outside, roll in quickly [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Bank follows groundspeed through each turn: if groundspeed is falling, keep reducing the bank; if it is rising, keep increasing it until the rollout [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Use the ground references, the nose and the wingtips together to place the airplane [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
Too close to the references forces steep banks, which raise the load factor and stall speed, especially in the turn after the downwind leg [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

body.p: What the maneuver trains (and what you grade): holding a set relation to the ground, dividing attention, adjusting bank for groundspeed, rolling out with the correct wind correction angle, and preparing for the traffic pattern [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Turn timing is part of it: failing to execute turns with accurate timing is on the AFH error list for this maneuver [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

callout.text: Patter idea (application): on downwind, say the wind out loud before every corner: 'tailwind now, becoming a crosswind from the left: steep roll-in, then easing off, nose toward the inside.' The learner hears the reasoning, not just the bank numbers.

check.q: On the rectangular course, the wind will drift the airplane toward the inside of the course during the next turn. How should the roll-in look?
check.a: Slow. When the wind could drift the airplane into the course, the roll rate should be slow; when it could drift it outside, quick [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

chunks.title: Rectangular course and the traffic pattern

body.p: Relationship of rectangular course to airport traffic pattern: the rectangular course exists to replicate the pattern an airplane flies to land, and to prepare the pilot for pattern and landing practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. The legs, the crab on the crosswind legs and the changing bank in the turns are the same skills. Traffic Patterns (AI.VI.B) covers wind correction leg by leg in the real pattern; teach the rectangular course as the safe rehearsal for it.

head: Rectangular course
Airport traffic pattern
rows: Normally 45° to the downwind leg, toward a point abeam midfield [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
One-half to three-fourths of a mile from the field boundaries [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Downwind about one-half to 1 mile from the runway [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Propeller airplanes enter at 1,000 feet AGL unless the airport says otherwise [[33:239|AIM 4-3-3]]
Crab into the wind to keep the track parallel to the field edge [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]
Track perpendicular to the extended centerline, nose turned into the wind as needed [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
Constant altitude and airspeed all the way around [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Power reduction, descent, configuration changes and a runway to line up with [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]

body.p: Aim for correlation. The AIH calls the correlation level, where the learner links a block of learning with other skills, the objective of aviation instruction, and its example is relating turn entries to performance in traffic patterns [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. A learner who can fly a tidy rectangle but cannot explain why the downwind-to-base turn in the pattern needs more bank on a windy day has not reached it.

callout.text: Bridge it in the air (application): after a good rectangular course, ask the learner to fly the same rectangle around the runway of a nearby quiet field, then talk through what will change when power comes back abeam the numbers.

check.q: Your learner flies a good rectangular course but cannot say how it relates to landing patterns. Which AIH level of learning is missing?
check.a: Correlation, the level where the learner associates what was taught with other skills, such as turn entries with traffic pattern performance; the AIH calls it the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

chunks.title: S-turns: entry, wind correction and the reversal

body.p: S-turns: two opposite but equal half-circles on each side of a straight line [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Enter perpendicular to the line, as the ACS requires (ACS AI.IX.E.S3b), from the downwind position: cross the line at 90° and immediately begin a 180° constant-radius turn [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].

bullets: First half (downwind side): roll in rapidly but not aggressively to the steepest bank, then decrease the bank and the rollout rate as groundspeed falls [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].
At the 90° point the airplane is directly crosswind and must have the right wind correction angle [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].

Reverse the turn directly over the selected reference line (ACS AI.IX.E.S5): time the rollout so the wings come level just as the airplane crosses the line at the proper heading, altitude and airspeed, with no delay before the opposite turn [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].
Second half (upwind side): the roll-in is smooth and gentle with a shallow bank, then the bank increases as the turn swings downwind and groundspeed builds [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].
Repeat as many as can be safely flown along the line [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].

body.p: The heading puzzle learners stumble on: the airplane turns a different number of degrees in the air than over the ground. In the AFH example, with a 10° wind correction angle needed at the crosswind point, the first 90° of ground track takes 100° of heading change and the last 90° only 80° [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. Draw it on the board before the flight.

callout.text: Build it in pieces. The AIH example for a learner who is struggling: start S-turns with headings only, then add altitude control, drift correction and coordination one at a time [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

check.q: During S-turns your learner rolls wings level a few hundred feet before the road and flies straight across it. Which ACS item is missed and what is the cue?
check.a: S5: the turn must reverse directly over the reference line (ACS AI.IX.E.S5). Cue: adjust the rollout timing so the wings come level just as the airplane crosses the line, then roll straight into the next turn with no delay [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

chunks.title: Turns around a point: entry, either direction, and the view

body.p: Turns around a point: consecutive 360° constant-radius turns around one point, a logical extension of the rectangular course and S-turns [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Enter at an appropriate distance from the reference point (ACS AI.IX.E.S3c), downwind, where groundspeed is fastest, at the planned radius [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. At least one 360° turn is required, but two or more let the pilot properly assess the wind and the bank needed [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

bullets: Roll-in: in a strong wind, roll in quickly so the steepest bank is set before the airplane drifts outside the radius [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Then shallow the bank gradually until headed directly upwind, and steepen it again through crosswind to downwind, reaching the steepest bank back at the entry point [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Heading versus position: in the downwind half the heading moves toward the inside of the turn (ahead of the position); in the upwind half, toward the outside (behind it) [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

Either direction: the ACS lets the evaluator specify the direction (ACS AI.IX.E.S5). In a high-wing airplane the lowered wing can hide the point, especially in left turns flown from the left seat; change the altitude or the radius so the point stays in sight [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

body.p: Turns around a point add something the other two do not: bank changes that never stop, because the wind direction changes all the way around [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. That is why the AFH lists 'managing the quickly-changing bank angles' and compensating for drift in quickly-changing orientations among its objectives [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

callout.text: Practice both directions yourself from the right seat (application). The AFH notes the wing problem for a left-seat pilot in left turns [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]; in the right seat, your blind turns are the right ones. Find the radius and altitude that keep the point in view for both of you.

check.q: Halfway through the upwind half of a turn around a point, where should the nose point compared with the airplane's position over the ground?
check.a: Behind its position, toward the outside of the turn. In the downwind half it is the opposite: ahead of its position, toward the inside [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

body.p: Order the lesson in blocks. Start with tracking over a straight line and an offset parallel path [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], then the rectangular course, then the turning maneuvers; turns around a point build on both the rectangular course and S-turns [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. On the ground, cover wind and drift, groundspeed and bank, the entry plan for the maneuver of the day, the safety plan, and the errors you will be watching for.

head: Point in the maneuver
Sample patter for turns around a point (application)
Basis
rows: 'Clear left, right, above and below. 800 feet, cruise speed set. That field is our engine-out field.'
'Wind on our tail, highest groundspeed: steepest bank, rolling in briskly.'
'Groundspeed falling, easing the bank. Nose stays ahead of our position.'
'Groundspeed building, steepening. Nose now behind our position, toward the outside.'

bullets: Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, safety steps included, in the order you briefed it, and admit any place your demo strays from your words [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
When the learner talks you through it while you fly, a misunderstanding about the wind shows up before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Do not stop at 'can fly it': the AIH's wind drift example ends with a learner who is only capable of performing the maneuver [[25:66|AIH 3-15]], or only of practicing it with help [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].
Test understanding by changing it: a new reference, the other direction, or reversing course after a series of S-turns [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
Teach the wind theory on the ground. Low over the fields the learner's attention belongs on flying; teaching at the wrong time creates hazards [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Your own talk can steal your lookout. The AIH warns that an instructor passing a lot of information can lose track of collision avoidance and situational awareness [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. At 800 feet AGL keep the patter short.

check.q: Why fly the straight-line and offset-line tracking before the first rectangular course?
check.a: The AFH introduces ground reference work by correcting for crosswind over a straight line, then on a parallel offset path no more than three-fourths of a mile away [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Drift correction is learned alone before turns and changing bank are added, the same reason the AIH breaks S-turns into elements [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and situational awareness

body.p: Division of attention between aircraft control and orientation is the core skill of the Task. The pilot holds attitude while tracking a path, scans for traffic and other hazards, keeps an emergency landing in mind, and checks flight and engine instruments now and then so a dropping oil pressure does not become a surprise [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

bullets: Fixating on one reference, such as one spot on the ground or horizon, destroys the ability to judge rate. Scan across several references to see closure and drift [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Fixation often means the task got too little practice alone; make sure each task can be done reasonably well in isolation before combining them [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
Spot it by following the learner's eyes: a long stare at one thing suggests fixation, and eyes that never visit the engine gauges suggest inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Point out fixation and inattention when they occur [[25:83|AIH 3-32]].

body.p: Distractions and task prioritization: the AIH distraction list includes identifying ground objects, identifying a field for a forced landing, and reversing course after a series of S-turns [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Use them on purpose, once the maneuver is solid, and watch what slips first. Task prioritization in this Task means airplane control and the lookout come before a perfect track (application).

Loss of situational awareness covers the airplane's position, flight path, other aircraft and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Disorientation here is usually losing the wind: after several circles the learner no longer knows which side is downwind or where the emergency field is. Failing to properly assess wind direction is on all three AFH error lists [[24:153|AFH 7-7]] [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

callout.text: Orientation check (application): mid-maneuver, ask 'Where is the wind from, and where would we land if the engine quit now?' A pause before the answer tells you the learner is flying the shape by habit.

check.q: During turns around a point your learner's eyes stay on the silo for a whole circle while altitude drifts 80 feet. How do you know it is fixation and what do you do?
check.a: A long stare at one thing suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Point it out [[25:83|AIH 3-32]], teach the scan across several references and the horizon [[24:147|AFH 7-1]], and if needed practice the altitude task alone before combining again [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

body.p: Collision hazards: ground reference maneuvers put the airplane low, among other aircraft including helicopters, and near obstructions such as radio towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Clear the area with two 90° clearing turns, looking left and right as well as above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. A clearing turn makes sure the next maneuver will not head into another airplane's path; teach a clearing procedure and insist on its use [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Have the learner call it aloud: 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Scan in short eye movements of no more than 10°, at least 1 second each [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Traffic with no relative motion that stays in one scan quadrant is likely on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Make radio calls on a practice area frequency if there is one [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Clearing is not only at the start: failing to clear the area initially and throughout the maneuver is the first error on every AFH list [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

body.p: Why it matters at this altitude: in the AIH midair study, most collisions happened at or near nontowered airports at altitudes below 1,000 feet, mostly in good weather and daylight, and a flight instructor was aboard in 37 percent of them [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. A learner who thinks the instructor does all the looking never builds the habit; correct any maneuver started without a traffic check at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Application: the lowered wing in a turn around a point blocks a slice of sky on every circle, and both pilots are looking at the ground. Build the lookout into each quarter of the circle, not just the entry.

check.q: Why does the AIH midair study make ground reference maneuvers a lookout lesson as much as a wind lesson?
check.a: Most midair collisions in the study happened near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet in good weather, with an instructor aboard in 37 percent [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], which describes a typical ground reference lesson.

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin, CFIT and uncoordinated flight

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering: these maneuvers are flown at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, where an engine failure leaves less time to configure and less gliding distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Keep one or more emergency landing spots in mind [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

bullets: Stall: stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. A level 45° turn is 1.41 G; an airplane that stalls at 50 knots level stalls at 60 knots at 45° and 70 knots at 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Accidental stalls in steep turns or with abrupt back elevator near the ground have caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Spin: a stall in a slipping or skidding turn can become a spin in the direction of the rudder applied, whichever wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT): an airworthy airplane, under the pilot's control, flown into terrain, an obstacle or water [[30:73|RMH G-1]]. It is one of the top four causes of fatal general aviation accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Here it looks like a learner sinking while staring at the point, or circling into a tower that was never spotted.

Situations that raise loss of control risk include uncoordinated flight and distraction [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and low-altitude maneuvering with uncoordinated flight or higher load factors deserves extra risk management [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

body.p: Uncoordinated flight: rudder must be used with aileron to counter adverse yaw, and holding uncoordinated control inputs creates the potential for a spin, especially at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. In a skid the pilot feels pushed to the outside of the turn, in a slip to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. The classic trap is the steep downwind turn: the airplane is swinging wide, the learner adds inside rudder to drag the nose around and back pressure to hold altitude. That is the setup for the skidding cross-control stall, which can roll toward inverted and begin a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Teach the exit, not the save: if the bank needed is too steep, leave the maneuver and set up farther out [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Never fix a wide circle with rudder.

check.q: Your learner is drifting outside the circle headed downwind and pushes inside rudder while pulling back. Why is that dangerous here?
check.a: Inside rudder with back pressure is a skidding, cross-controlled turn. A stall in a skid can roll the airplane and start a spin in the direction of the rudder [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and at 600 to 1,000 feet AGL there is little room to recover [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Exit and re-enter farther out instead [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

body.p: Common errors related to this Task: the AFH lists nine for the rectangular course and eight each for turns around a point and S-turns, nearly the same list [[24:153|AFH 7-7]] [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. For S8 the evaluator will fly some of them as your learner: name what you see, the likely cause, and the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to clear the area, initially and throughout
Maneuver started straight from cruise, no head movement during the circles
Two 90° clearing turns, called aloud, and a scan every quarter [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
No constant, level altitude before entry
Learner rolls in while still settling, and the altitude is never stable
Set altitude and airspeed, then enter [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]
Climbs on shallow-bank parts, sinks in the steep ones
Hold enough back pressure to keep the vertical component of lift; correct pitch on the natural horizon and cross-check the altimeter [[24:77|AFH 3-16]] (ACS AI.IX.E.S7)
Enters upwind, or steepest bank in the wrong place
Find the wind before entry [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] and enter downwind [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Rectangle legs bow in or out; S-turn halves unequal
Hold the angle that stops the drift on the references [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]
Same bank all the way around; circle slides downwind
Steepen as groundspeed rises, shallow as it falls [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]
Ball off center; learner feels pushed sideways
Eyes stuck on one reference; altitude or traffic missed
Scan several references [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]; practice weak tasks alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Turns start late, so the next leg starts wide or close
Start each turn at the boundary [[24:152|AFH 7-6]] and adjust roll rate for the wind [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]

body.p: How to analyze: when the learner talks while flying, you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; here, set the limit by altitude and bank before the flight. To reteach, demonstrate again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Read the shape (application): a circle that bulges on the downwind side means too little bank there; an S-turn whose second half is smaller than the first usually means the upwind roll-in was too steep.

check.q: As your learner, the evaluator flies a rectangular course where every corner starts late and each new leg begins wide. Which listed error is it, and what do you say?
check.a: Failure to execute turns with accurate timing, on the AFH rectangular course list [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. Cue: start each turn at the boundary [[24:152|AFH 7-6]], and adjust the roll rate for the wind: slow when drifting in, quick when drifting out [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-1. Wind drift. (AFH 7-3)
f1.alt: Six panels. Top row: a boat crossing a river with no current goes straight across; with a current it drifts downstream along a red dashed line; angled upstream it stays on the yellow course line. Bottom row: an airplane over a road with no wind stays over it; with wind from the left it drifts off to the right; crabbed into the wind it stays over the road.

f2.caption: Figure 7-2. Effect of wind during a turn. (AFH 7-4)
f2.alt: Two airplanes turn across a road. On the left, with no wind, the orange ground path is a neat half-circle. On the right, with a 20-knot wind blowing up the page, the actual ground path is wider and stretched compared with the dashed intended ground path.

f3.caption: Figure 7-4. Rectangular course. (AFH 7-6)
f3.alt: A rectangular field seen from above with the wind blowing right to left. The airplane enters 45 degrees to the downwind leg at top, then flies base, upwind and crosswind legs, crabbing into the wind on base and crosswind. Labels mark where turns start and end at the boundaries, which turns are more or less than 90 degrees, and dotted tracks show the drift with no wind correction.

f4.caption: Figure 8-1. Traffic Patterns (AFH 8-2)
f4.alt: Two perspective views of a runway with a red rectangular traffic pattern. The top shows a left-hand pattern and the bottom a right-hand pattern, each with entry, downwind, base, final, departure and crosswind legs labeled and a wind arrow.

f5.caption: Figure 7-6. S-turns. (AFH 7-9)
f5.alt: A straight road runs across the page with a crossroad at right. The wind blows up the page. An airplane enters at bottom right headed up, crosses the road, and flies a half-circle above the road and a half-circle below it, with numbered positions 1 to 5 and labels for steepest, moderate and shallowest bank and wings level over the road.

f6.caption: Figure 7-5. Turns around a point. (AFH 7-8)
f6.alt: An orange circle around a clump of trees with the wind blowing down the page. A dashed line divides the circle into an upwind half and a downwind half. Labels mark the steepest bank on the right, the shallowest bank on the left, a steeper bank at top and a shallower bank at bottom.

f7.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f7.alt: Three panels. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the outside. Coordinated turn: ball centered and the force straight down into the seat. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the inside.

scenario.title: CFI checkride: S-turns, then turns around a point
scenario.setup: On your CFI practical test the evaluator picks S-turns, then turns around a point, and plays a private pilot learner with 18 hours. You fly a high-wing trainer from the right seat. Terrain is farmland at 800 feet MSL, the wind at 1,000 feet AGL is about 18 knots from the west, a straight county road runs north and south, and a small town with a grain elevator lies two miles east. A crop-spraying helicopter has been working fields nearby.

questions.q: How and where do you set up the S-turns?
questions.a: Clear with two 90° turns [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], then enter perpendicular to the north-south road (ACS AI.IX.E.S3b) from the downwind position, headed east with the west wind on the tail [[24:155|AFH 7-9]], between 1,400 and 1,800 feet MSL (600 to 1,000 feet AGL over 800-foot terrain) (ACS AI.IX.E.S3b), at least 500 feet above and 2,000 feet from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

questions.q: What do you say at the first crosswind point of the demonstration?
questions.a: Something like: 'We are directly crosswind now, groundspeed falling, bank coming off, and the nose is angled into the wind ahead of our position.' At the 90° point the airplane must have the correct wind correction angle [[24:155|AFH 7-9]], and the AIH asks you to explain the factors while demonstrating [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

questions.q: The evaluator, as learner, crosses the road still in a 20° bank each time, and the second half-circle is smaller than the first. Analyze and correct it.
questions.a: The reversal is not over the line (ACS AI.IX.E.S5): the rollout is late, so the wings are not level as the airplane crosses [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. The smaller upwind half suggests the roll-in was too steep on the upwind side, where it should be smooth, gentle and shallow [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]. Cue the rollout timing against the road and the shallow upwind entry.

questions.q: For turns around a point the learner picks the grain elevator in town 'because it is easy to see.' What do you teach?
questions.a: The area should be well away from congested areas of a town [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and over one 14 CFR requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]], more than this maneuver's altitude. Pick a point over open fields with an emergency landing spot nearby [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

questions.q: Headed east in the turn around the new point, the circle swings wide and the learner adds left rudder and back pressure. What do you do?
questions.a: Headed east is downwind, so the bank should be steepest there [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Inside rudder with back pressure is a skid that can lead to a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Have the learner coordinate, and if the bank needed is too steep, exit and set up farther from the point [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

questions.q: You spot the helicopter low over a field about a mile ahead of the circle. How do you handle it?
questions.a: The AFH says to look specifically for helicopters during these maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Point it out, have the learner keep it in the scan, and if it shows no relative motion, take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Make sure the learner, not just you, owns the lookout [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver and throughout it, explaining your clearing as you do it.
skills.practice: Fly two 90° clearing turns before every ground reference maneuver and say 'clear left, right, above and below' aloud [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Select a suitable ground reference area, line, or point, and explain why it is safe and suitable: away from people, livestock and obstructions, with an emergency landing spot.
skills.practice: On every local flight, name a usable field, road and point for each maneuver and the forced landing field you would use [[24:147|AFH 7-1]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Plan the maneuver the evaluator picks: a rectangular course entered 45° to the downwind leg, S-turns entered perpendicular to the line, or turns around a point entered at an appropriate distance, all 600 to 1,000 feet AGL and at an appropriate distance from the selected reference area.
skills.practice: Brief each entry out loud on the ground with today's wind, including where the steepest bank will be [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

skills.do: Apply adequate wind-drift correction in straight and turning flight so the track around the rectangle stays constant, or the radius stays constant on each side of the line or around the point, while explaining the bank and crab changes.
skills.practice: Fly the AFH road demonstration with a constant bank, then fly the same turn varying the bank, and compare the ground tracks [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

skills.do: In S-turns, reverse directly over the reference line; in turns around a point, turn in whichever direction the evaluator specifies.
skills.practice: Practice turns around a point to the right from the right seat until the point stays in view [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

skills.do: Divide attention between airplane control, traffic avoidance and the ground track while keeping the ball centered, and keep talking without losing the lookout.
skills.practice: Record yourself flying and talking, then check how often your patter mentioned traffic and the ball (application).

skills.do: Maintain altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots while demonstrating.
skills.practice: Fly each maneuver silently first, then while explaining, and see if the altitude still holds.

skills.do: Watch the evaluator fly a flawed maneuver as your learner, name the error, explain its cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Have another CFI fly the AFH error list at you one item at a time while you diagnose it [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, when should a pilot be introduced to ground reference maneuvers?
options: After the first solo, once the pattern is mastered
As soon as the pilot shows proficiency in the four fundamentals
After the pilot has completed slow flight and stall training
Only after the pilot has learned steep turns
quiz.why: The instructor should introduce them as soon as the pilot shows proficiency in the four fundamentals [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

quiz.q: On a calm day your learner sets up turns around a very large grain bin and keeps ending up farther out than planned. Which AFH illusion best explains it?
options: Larger objects can appear closer than they really are, compared with smaller ones
Haze makes a reference appear closer than it would on a clear day with good visibility
Rain makes the airplane seem lower than it really is, so the learner climbs and widens out
A lower altitude makes the ground seem to pass more slowly, so turns are started late
quiz.why: Larger objects may appear closer than they are when compared with smaller ones, so the learner sets up too far out. The other three are reversed: clear air, not haze, makes references look closer; rain can make you feel higher; and lower altitudes make the ground seem to pass faster [[24:147|AFH 7-1]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

quiz.q: How far from the reference line does the AFH allow the offset parallel path when first teaching drift correction?
options: No more than one-quarter of a mile
No more than three-fourths of a mile
No more than one-half of a mile
No more than one mile
quiz.why: The offset parallel path should be no more than three-fourths of a mile from the reference line [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: Which AFH reason explains a steeper bank where groundspeed is higher during a constant-radius turn?
options: The wind lifts the upwind wing, which must be countered with more bank
The airspeed rises downwind, so a steeper bank is needed to hold altitude
There is less time to turn, so a higher rate of turn is needed
The load factor drops downwind, so more bank is safe there
quiz.why: At higher groundspeed there is less time to turn; the pilot banks more to increase the rate of turn [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner is discouraged by S-turns. What does the AIH suggest starting with?
options: Altitude control alone, with the instructor handling the wind
The full maneuver at a higher altitude to reduce the pressure
Headings only, adding the other elements one at a time
Turns around a point first, since one point is easier than a line
quiz.why: The AIH example: instruction in S-turns may begin with headings only, then add altitude control, drift correction and coordination one at a time [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

quiz.q: As part of preflight planning for ground reference maneuvers, which stall speed does the AFH tell the pilot to look up in the POH/AFM?
options: The stall speed at 30° of bank, the bank most of these maneuvers are flown at
The wings-level clean stall speed, since the bank stays at or under 45° anyway
The stall speed at 60° of bank, the same figure used for the steep turn briefing
The stall speed at 50° of bank, or at the highest bank angle expected in the maneuver
quiz.why: Preflight planning should include the predicted (POH/AFM) stall speed at 50° or at the highest bank angle expected, to assure a safety margin above the stall [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

quiz.q: How many 360° turns does the AFH suggest flying in turns around a point to properly assess the wind?
options: One complete turn is enough to judge the wind
Exactly three, the same as the steep spiral
Half a turn, then exit and re-enter downwind
Two or more, though at least one is required
quiz.why: At least one 360° turn is needed, but to properly assess wind and bank the pilot should complete two or more [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

quiz.q: In the AIH midair collision study, where did the vast majority of accidents occur?
options: At or near nontowered airports and at altitudes below 1,000 feet
In Class B airspace at cruise altitudes above 3,000 feet
On instrument approaches in marginal visibility
Over practice areas at altitudes between 3,000 and 5,000 feet
quiz.why: The vast majority occurred at or near nontowered airports and below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

quiz.q: As a general note, what limits does the AFH give for any ground reference maneuver?
options: Bank no more than 30° and airspeed no more than normal cruise speed
Bank no more than 60° and airspeed no more than VNO
Bank no more than 45° and airspeed no more than maneuvering speed
Bank no more than 45° and airspeed no more than VNO
quiz.why: A ground reference maneuver should not exceed 45° of bank or an airspeed greater than the maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

quiz.q: Which error is on the AFH rectangular course list but not on its S-turns or turns around a point lists?
options: Failure to execute turns with accurate timing
Failure to properly assess wind direction
Failure to maintain altitude during the maneuver
Failure to apply coordinated aileron and rudder pressure
quiz.why: Turn timing (and division of attention) appear only on the rectangular course list [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]; the other three are on all of them [[24:154|AFH 7-8]] [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: During your S8 demonstration the evaluator, as learner, enters turns around a point at 800 feet AGL, sinks to 690 feet AGL in the steep part, and runs 9 knots fast. What do you call out?
options: Nothing; both are within the CFI and private ACS tolerances for this Task
Only the airspeed, which is outside the ±5 knot limit
Both, since 690 feet is below the 700-foot ACS floor
Only the altitude, 110 feet low; the airspeed is within limits
final_quiz.why: The ACS allows altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.IX.E.S7). 800 - 690 = 110 feet low is outside; 9 knots fast is inside. Failing to maintain altitude is a listed error [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator asks for turns around a point to the right. You fly a high-wing trainer with side-by-side seats from the right seat. What should you expect and plan for?
options: Right turns are easiest from the right seat, since you look down past the raised wing
The lowered right wing may hide the point from you; adjust the altitude or radius to keep it in view
Turn direction makes no difference in a high-wing; only the bank angle decides whether the point hides
Ask the evaluator for left turns instead, since the ACS lets the applicant pick the direction
final_quiz.why: The AFH describes the lowered wing of a high-wing airplane hiding the point in left turns flown from the left seat, and says to change the altitude or the radius [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]; from the right seat the same happens in right turns (application). The evaluator, not the applicant, specifies the direction (ACS AI.IX.E.S5).

final_quiz.q: You fly a left-hand rectangular course with the wind from the west, so the downwind leg runs east along the south side. On the leg that runs south along the west side, where is the nose pointed?
options: Angled west, toward the outside of the course
Angled east, toward the inside of the course
Straight south, since the wind is behind the airplane
Angled south-east, toward the next corner
final_quiz.why: That leg has the wind from the right, drifting the airplane east into the course, so the pilot holds an angle into the wind, toward the outside [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner insists that a constant-bank turn draws a round ground track in any wind. Which AFH demonstration shows the effect most directly?
options: Over a road perpendicular to the wind, fly a 360° steep turn; you finish right over the start point if the bank is held
Fly one turn around a point at a constant 30° of bank; the circle stays round as long as the ball is centered
Over a road parallel to the wind, headed into it, fly a 360° medium-bank turn; you finish downwind of the start
Track the road headed downwind with no crab; the airplane stays over the road, showing the bank alone sets the track
final_quiz.why: The AFH demonstration: over a straight road parallel to the wind, fly into the wind, then make a 360° constant medium-banked turn. The airplane returns over the road but downwind from the start; the path over the ground is not circular, though through the air it is [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

final_quiz.q: Entering turns around a point downwind in a strong wind, your learner rolls in slowly and is outside the radius by the crosswind point. What does the AFH say?
options: Roll in slowly anyway and correct by turning less on the upwind side
Enter on the upwind side instead so the roll-in can be gentle
Roll in quickly so the steepest bank is set before any drift
Hold a medium bank on the first circle and fix the radius on the second
final_quiz.why: Depending on the wind, it may be necessary to roll in at a rapid rate so the steepest bank is set quickly and the airplane does not drift outside the radius [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: How does the AIH suggest you find out whether your learner is fixating during turns around a point?
options: Ask the learner after each circle which instruments and references were checked
Glance at the learner's eyes to see where the learner is looking
Count how many times the learner moves the yoke per circle
Cover the attitude indicator and see if the bank wanders
final_quiz.why: One way is to glance at the learner's eyes; a long look at one thing may mean fixation. It has limits, since looking is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies smooth S-turns. Which AIH distraction is built from this very maneuver?
options: Have the learner fly the S-turns with the ball held off center
Have the learner tune the practice area frequency mid-turn
Have the learner reverse course after a series of S-turns
Have the learner close the eyes for one half-circle
final_quiz.why: The AIH distraction list includes having the learner reverse course after a series of S-turns [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: Before a turn around a point, what does the AIH suggest you prompt the learner to identify aloud?
options: The wind correction angle at each quarter of the circle
The heading at each crosswind point and the wind correction angle needed there
The expected bank angle at the steepest point of the circle
Potential collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing
final_quiz.why: While preparing to fly a ground reference maneuver, ask the learner to identify potential collision hazards and a safe emergency landing place [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner skids in the steep downwind turn and stalls. Which way does the AFH say a spin from a skidding or slipping turn will rotate?
options: Away from the rudder, toward the raised wing
Always toward the lowered wing
Opposite to the aileron, whichever way the bank is
In the direction of the rudder applied, whichever wingtip is raised
final_quiz.why: A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can result in a spin entry and rotation in the direction of rudder application, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: How does the distance from the field on a rectangular course compare with the downwind leg of a traffic pattern?
options: Both are flown exactly one-half mile out so the transfer is direct
The course one-half to three-fourths mile out; the pattern downwind about one-half to 1 mile
The course is flown 1 to 2 miles out; the pattern downwind is flown about one-half mile out
The course is flown directly over the boundaries; the pattern downwind is offset one full mile
final_quiz.why: The rectangular course is flown one-half to three-fourths of a mile from the boundaries [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]; the pattern downwind is about one-half to 1 mile from the runway [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

final_quiz.q: Before S-turns, your learner works the wind correction angle on an E6B. What does the AFH say about drift correction in these maneuvers?
options: Pilots don't calculate it; they adjust using the references
Compute it first so the right crab is held at each crosswind point
Compute it only when the wind is stronger than 15 knots
Use the GPS track and heading to set it before entry
final_quiz.why: Pilots do not calculate the drift correction angles for ground reference maneuvers; they use the references and adjust to cancel drift [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

final_quiz.q: At about 900 feet AGL over farmland, which hazards does the AFH specifically remind you to look for?
options: Large jets descending to nearby airports and military low-level routes
Other aircraft including helicopters, plus towers and wires
Parachute jumpers and gliders working ridge lift above the practice area
Balloons and banner tow aircraft operating below 500 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: Pilots should look for other aircraft, including helicopters, and obstructions such as radio towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to fly turns around a point at 500 feet AGL 'to see the drift better.' Besides the ACS entry band, which AFH altitude point argues against it?
options: After an engine failure, a lower altitude leaves less time to configure and less gliding distance
Below 600 feet AGL the AFH lowers its bank limit for these maneuvers from 45° to 30°
Wind correction angles grow sharply near the ground, so the circle cannot be held at that height
Lower altitudes make the airplane seem to move more slowly over the ground, which hides the drift
final_quiz.why: The AFH altitude considerations include that lower altitudes mean less time to configure the airplane and reduced gliding distance before a forced landing; lower altitudes also make the airplane seem faster over the ground, not slower [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. The ACS entry band is 600 to 1,000 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.E.S3c).

takeaways: Purpose: fly a set path over the ground while dividing attention, the base skill for every traffic pattern.
Standard: enter 600 to 1,000 feet AGL, altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots; the same words as the private ACS.
Wind: crab to stop drift on straight legs; bank follows groundspeed in turns, steepest downwind, shallowest upwind.
Rectangular course: 45° entry to downwind, one-half to three-fourths mile out, roll slowly when drifting in, quickly when drifting out.
S-turns: enter perpendicular to the line headed downwind; wings level right over the line, then straight into the opposite turn.
Turns around a point: enter downwind at the planned radius, either direction as specified, and keep the point in view.
Risks: low altitude, traffic, wires, fixation and skidding turns; if the bank gets too steep, exit and move out.
cfi_notes: The CFI and private ACS use identical S1 to S7 words (ACS AI.IX.E, PA.V.B). The CFI Task adds 'procedures' to K1, K5 common errors, S8, and 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains'.

The ACS sets no bank limit for this Task. The AFH gives 45° as a general limit for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]; brief it as the AFH guidance, not as an ACS tolerance.

AFH 7-4 says the radius of turn in the air 'varies proportionally with the bank angle' [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. The PHAK formula shows radius goes down as the tangent of bank goes up [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]; teach the formula, and read the AFH line as 'bank sets radius'.
The ACS enters the rectangular course 45° to the downwind leg (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a); the AFH text says enter downwind and its figure shows the 45° entry [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. They agree.

The ACS says only 'appropriate distance' for S-turns and turns around a point. The one AFH distance number, one-half to three-fourths of a mile, is for the rectangular course [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]; for the turning maneuvers, size the radius so the downwind bank stays at or under 45°.

The AIH's own wind drift lesson plan ends with a learner who can only practice the maneuver with help [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Plan follow-up lessons that take it to correlation with the traffic pattern [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].
The pattern downwind is about one-half to 1 mile out [[24:167|AFH 8-3]], a little wider than the rectangular course's one-half to three-fourths mile [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Expect a learner to ask why.
Point learners to AI.IV.A for the corner-by-corner rectangular course briefing and AI.VI.B for wind correction in the real pattern; this lesson does not repeat them.

Practice right turns around a point from the right seat before the checkride: the AFH describes the blocked view for a left-seat pilot in left turns [[24:154|AFH 7-8]], and the mirror image applies to you (application).
gaps: No source gives an airspeed for these maneuvers; the ACS holds you to ±10 knots of the one you choose. Use the POH/AFM and stay at or below maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
No source gives a radius for S-turns or turns around a point; plan it from your groundspeed and bank limit.
The stall speed at 45° or 50° of bank for your airplane comes from the POH/AFM [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

The sources do not say how to estimate the wind at maneuvering altitude beyond surface clues and watching the drift [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]; a winds aloft forecast or GPS groundspeed check is the CFI's call.
Local practice area frequencies and preferred areas come from local knowledge and the Chart Supplement, not from these handbooks.

activities.title: Read the S-turns
activities.intro: The wind blows up the page. Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: First crossing of the line at 90°, headed downwind
Directly crosswind on the first turn: wind correction angle set

Directly crosswind on the second turn: groundspeed now building

activities.title: Plan the circle for today's wind
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. Radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tan bank), with groundspeed in knots for the radius over the ground. Rate of turn = 1,091 x tan bank / true airspeed in knots.

items.q: You hold a constant 25° bank around a point. Airspeed 80 knots, wind 15 knots, so groundspeed is 95 knots headed downwind and 65 knots headed upwind. How many feet wider is the radius over the ground at the downwind point than at the upwind point?
items.why: 11.26 x tan 25° = 11.26 x 0.4663 = 5.251. Downwind 95 x 95 / 5.251 = 9,025 / 5.251 = 1,719 ft; upwind 65 x 65 / 5.251 = 4,225 / 5.251 = 805 ft; 1,719 - 805 = 914 ft [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. That is the egg shape: with a fixed bank the radius grows with groundspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

items.q: Rate of turn uses airspeed, not groundspeed. At 80 knots true airspeed, say the steep downwind point of the circle needs 38° of bank. What is the rate of turn there, in degrees per second?
items.why: 1,091 x tan 38° / 80 = 1,091 x 0.7813 / 80 = 852.4 / 80 = 10.7° per second [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. The steeper bank raises the rate of turn to make up for the shorter time at high groundspeed [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

items.q: Same 80 knots true airspeed, now at the shallow upwind point with 21° of bank. What is the rate of turn?
items.why: 1,091 x tan 21° / 80 = 1,091 x 0.3839 / 80 = 418.8 / 80 = 5.2° per second, about half the downwind rate [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. At low groundspeed the pilot shallows the bank and slows the rate to match the extra time [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

items.q: Why the rates differ: how many more seconds does the airplane take to cover 1,000 feet of ground track headed upwind (65 knots groundspeed) than headed downwind (95 knots groundspeed)? One nautical mile is 6,076.1 feet.

activities.title: Fly one pair of S-turns
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Clear the area with two 90° clearing turns
Set a constant, level altitude and airspeed
Cross the line at 90°, headed downwind
Roll in briskly to the steepest bank, then ease it as groundspeed falls
Wings level just as the airplane re-crosses the line
Roll gently into a shallow opposite turn, steepening as groundspeed builds

activities.title: True or false: choosing and clearing
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: On a hazy day a reference tends to look closer than it does on a clear day.
cards.why: False. Excellent visibility with clear skies makes a reference look closer than on a hazy day [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

cards.s: Rain can create the illusion of being higher than you actually are.
The lower the maneuvering altitude, the faster the airplane seems to move over the ground.
The AFH says to clear the area only before entering the maneuver.
cards.why: False. Failing to clear the area initially and throughout the maneuver is a listed error [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

cards.s: Before a ground reference maneuver, the AFH includes radio announcements, such as on a practice area frequency.
cards.why: True, along with the checklist and clearing turns [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

cards.s: If straight-and-level traffic stays in one spot on the windshield, it is moving parallel to you and is no threat.
cards.why: False. No relative motion while staying in one scan quadrant means a likely collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

activities.title: A windy rectangular course lesson
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your private learner has 12 hours and is solid on the four fundamentals. The wind at 1,000 feet AGL is about 20 knots from the south. You chose a square section of farmland with roads on all four sides, terrain at 600 feet MSL.

steps.s: Over the practice area there is no windsock in sight, and the learner asks how to confirm the wind direction before choosing the entry.
options: Use the heading indicator: the wind comes from the direction of the longest side of the field
Assume it matches the departure airport's wind from 40 miles away and enter on that basis
Use surface clues such as smoke, dust or wind patterns on water, then confirm by watching the drift
Skip it; on a rectangular course the entry direction makes no difference to the bank angles
steps.why: Wind direction and speed can be judged from smoke, dust, brush fires, wind farms or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]], and pilots adjust to cancel the drift they see on the references [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. The entry must be downwind so the steepest bank comes first [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

options: On the north side, headed north, 45° to the upwind leg
On the west side headed north, at 45° to that downwind leg
On the south side, headed south into the wind
On the east side, on a crosswind leg
steps.why: Enter 45° to the downwind leg (ACS AI.IX.E.S3a), with the wind on the tail [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. A south wind makes the downwind heading north.

steps.s: The learner held a crab into the wind on the base leg. Turning onto the upwind leg, the learner rolls into a steep bank and turns a little more than 90°.
options: Use a medium bank and turn less than 90°, because the airplane is already angled into the wind
Correct: the turn after the base leg is always the steepest of the four
Use a shallow bank rolled in slowly, and turn more than 90° to stay outside the field
Keep the wings level through the corner, then crab onto the new heading
steps.why: The base-to-upwind turn is a medium-banked turn, and because the pilot was angled into the wind on the base leg, the turn to the upwind leg is less than 90° [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

steps.s: Halfway around, the altimeter shows 1,480 feet MSL after the learner entered at 1,600 MSL, and the learner has not looked outside the turn for a while.
options: Ignore it; the track is the main skill today
Take the controls and fly the rest yourself
Coach altitude and lookout now: the learner is 120 feet low and fixating
Climb 500 feet and start over at a safer altitude
steps.why: The ACS allows ±100 feet (ACS AI.IX.E.S7); 1,600 - 1,480 = 120 feet. Point out fixation when it occurs [[25:83|AIH 3-32]] and keep the scan going, since clearing continues throughout [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

steps.s: Postflight, the learner asks what any of this has to do with landing.
options: Nothing directly; it only builds stick-and-rudder feel
It is only practice for the checkride
It prepares the learner for steep turns
It replicates the traffic pattern: same legs, same crab and bank changes
steps.why: The rectangular course replicates the airport traffic pattern and prepares the pilot for pattern and landing practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
